Authors Affiliation * 1 Universidade Cruzeiro do Sul, São Paulo, Brazil. * PMID: 36867588 * DOI: 10.1097/PEP.0000000000000999 Abstract Purpose: To summarize and update the current knowledge on the effectiveness of hippotherapy on postural control in children with cerebral palsy. Methods: Using a systematic review methodology, the electronic databases PubMed, Virtual Health Library, PEDro, Scielo, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for eligible articles from 2011 up to September 2021. Quality assessment of eligible studies was performed using the PEDro scale. Results: There were 239 identified studies. Eight clinical trials were selected. The total sample consisted of 264 individuals, with 134 allocated to the experimental group (hippotherapy) and 130 individuals to the control group (conventional therapy). Most studies had moderate to high methodological quality. Conclusions: Hippotherapy can be an effective intervention to improve several aspects related to postural control, such as static balance (especially in the sitting posture), dynamic balance, and alignment (body posture) in children aged 3 to 16 years, particularly with spastic hemiplegia or diplegia. fetched_contents.text: Effects of hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding on postural control or balance in children with cerebral palsy: a meta‐analysis - ZADNIKAR - 2011 - Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology Abbreviation THR Therapeutic horseback riding CP Cerebral palsy What this paper adds * • It is the first known meta-analysis of the literature on hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding in children with cerebral palsy. * • It gives an overview of the effects of hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding on postural control or balance. * • The meta-analysis found a statistically significant effect of hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding in children with cerebral palsy. Cerebral palsy (CP) is a term used to define a spectrum of syndromes of posture and motor impairment that results from an insult to the developing central nervous system.1 This syndrome includes the following components: aberrant control of movement and/or posture, early onset, and no recognizable underlying progressive pathology.2 Disorders of movement and posture are caused by damage to the motor cortex. The consequences of chronic muscle imbalance and the resultant deformities can cause increasing disability with age.3,4 In addition to postural and motor abnormalities, people with CP may exhibit secondary consequences of brain damage, including learning disability,* other cognitive and sensory impairments, speech and language disorders, orthopaedic complications, and epilepsy.5,6 One of the most significant problems in children with CP is defective postural control. Maintaining postural control, required for the performance of activities of daily living, is often a major challenge for children with CP.7–10 Postural control is organized at two functional levels.8–10 The first level consists of a direction-specific adjustment, when the equilibrium of the body is endangered, or the generation of direction-specific patterns of postural adjustment.9,10 For example, when reaching, the muscles on the dorsal side of the body are primarily activated when the body leans forwards, whereas the muscles on the ventral side of the body are primarily activated when the body leans in the opposite direction.7,10 According to van der Heide the second level of postural control is involved in the fine-tuning of the basic, direction-specific adjustment according to multisensorial afferent input from the somatosensory, visual, and vestibular systems. This modulation can be achieved in various ways, for instance, by changing the order in which the agonist muscles are recruited (e.g. in a caudal to cranial sequence or vice versa), by modifying the size of the muscle contraction, which is reflected in electromyography (EMG) amplitude, or by altering the degree of antagonist activation.10 Various approaches exist for improving postural control and balance, including neurodevelopmental treatment which is classified as a neurophysiological or neuromaturational therapeutic approach, as are Vojta therapy, Temple Fay, the Rood and Kabat methods, and sensory integration.9–11 Newer approaches, such as the ecological and dynamical system approaches, propose that development of motor skills and coordination occurs as the result of multifaceted interactions that take place in the context of performing a specific task.10,11 Other frequently evaluated therapeutic methods are conductive education and biofeedback with a central role for motor learning theories.11 Hippotherapy is also one of these approaches in which equine movement is used for its therapeutic effect.12 Therapeutic horseback riding and hippotherapy Riding may lead to improved coordination,13 increased head and trunk control,14 and improved gait.15,16 The rationale for hippotherapy is that the horse’s gait provides a precise, smooth, rhythmic, and repetitive pattern of movement to the rider that is similar to the mechanics of human gait.15,17 The horse’s centre of gravity is displaced three-dimensionally when walking, resulting in a movement that is very similar to that of the human pelvis during walking.17 This rhythmical movement, combined with the warmth of the horse, is hypothesized to decrease hypertonicity and promote relaxation in the rider with spastic CP.18 Adjusting to the horse’s movements also involves the use of muscles and joint movements which, over time, may lead to increased strength and range of motion.12,19 In general, the movement of the horse provides a variety of inputs to the rider, which may be used to facilitate improved contraction, joint stability, weight shift, and postural equilibrium responses in children with CP.6 Therapeutic horseback riding (THR) is a broad term that covers many elements of recreational horse riding. THR must be performed only by specially trained riding instructors and assistants. To ensure safety and effectiveness, the instructors, even though they are usually not medical professionals, should be aware of the rider’s state of health, contraindications, disabilities, and other limitations, and be competent to select, train, and prepare the appropriate horse.20,21 THR instructors and assistants must follow multifaceted lesson plans as THR sessions include many procedures and precautions. The THR instructor decides if a saddle is required and if the horse remains stationary or walks, while the child, following his directions, tries, for example, to touch different parts of the horse or reach for an object. The assistant provides help if needed, but this should not be restrictive.20,22 The horse is equipped with a bridle and a vaulting surcingle, which can be used as a handhold and to which auxiliary reins are attached. The exercises are aimed primarily at maintaining balance and proper body posture in different positions, at the development of the rider’s sensory–motor and perceptual–motor skills and at a gradual increase in the rider’s capacity to stretch and move while the horse moves at a slow, steady gait.20,22 The primary goal of…

fetched_contents.text: The effects of hippotherapy on postural balance and functional ability in children with cerebral palsy Abstract [Purpose] This study evaluated the effects of hippotherapy on seated postural balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance in children with cerebral palsy and compared the effects of 12 and 24 sessions on seated postural balance. [Subjects and Methods] This study included 15 children with cerebral palsy aged between 5 and 10 years. Interventions: A hippotherapy protocol was performed for 30 minutes, twice a week, for 12 weeks. Postural balance in a sitting position was measured using an AMTI AccuSway Plus force platform 1 week before initiating the hippotherapy program and after 12 and 24 weeks. The Berg Balance Scale (BBS) and Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory (PEDI) were used before and after 24 sessions. [Results] Significant differences were observed for center of pressure (COP) variables, including medio-lateral (COPml), anteroposterior displacement (COPap), and velocity of displacement (VelCOP), particularly after 24 sessions. There were also significant differences in BBS scores and PEDI score increases associated with functional skills (self-care, social function, and mobility), caregiver assistance (self-care), social function, and mobility. [Conclusion] Hippotherapy resulted in improvement in postural balance in the sitting position, dynamic balance, and functionality in children with cerebral palsy, an effect particularly significant after 24 hippotherapy sessions. Key words: Hippotherapy, Postural balance, Cerebral palsy INTRODUCTION Childhood diseases often affect development; among these diseases, chronic nonprogressive infantile encephalopathy—better known as cerebral palsy (CP)—is the most common, and generally results in disabilities due to abnormal motor control1). This disease is heterogeneous in both clinical presentation and etiology2, 3). Its clinical manifestations depend on the extent, type, and site of lesions in the central nervous system (CNS) as well as the CNS’s ability to adapt or reorganize in response to changes2, 3). Structural and mechanical changes in body alignment as well as musculoskeletal changes can occur in CP. Often, children with CP develop compensatory mechanisms to overcome gravity and recruit new muscle groups to maintain stability. However, long-term compensations lead to muscle imbalance, increased hypertonia, and deformities that affect postural balance, which is essential for development of complex motor skills and impacts functional activities, thus limiting participation in different activities4). Development of automatic postural reactions, including straightening, balance, and protection, may also be delayed or undeveloped5). The visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems behave as a multisensory network that helps to maintain posture and balance, and it may be affected in patients with CP. These systems, in combination with the cerebellar and musculoskeletal systems, are controlled by the CNS and are affected by experiences and environment6,7,8). Therefore, therapies such as hippotherapy may minimize the clinical aspects of the disease and improve postural balance. Previous studies have shown that hippotherapy can improve balance and daily functional activities in patients with CP9,10,11,12,13). Different methods, including functional tests and scales, have been used to assess the effects of hippotherapy on postural balance in patients with CP. Studies using stabilometry assessed by force platforms are less common13,14,15), and most involve the use of a static position and hippotherapy simulator. The use of this technique in combination with functional tests could permit a broader analysis of the effects of hippotherapy on postural balance. Postural balance assessment using a force platform in patients with CP in the sitting position16, 17), is less commonly performed than that in the standing position5, 18,19,20). The sitting position, however, is used more often by individuals with CP during daily activities because it uses less energy, provides better performance, or because individuals cannot maintain a standing position. In addition, this position is similar to that used in hippotherapy because the child remains seated on the horse during the session and experiences movements produced by the horse’s gait. Moreover, there is still no consensus in the literature regarding the number of hippotherapy sessions necessary to change the postural balance in individuals with CP. Findings in previous studies varied from one21) to 40 sessions22). The most common treatments included 10–12 sessions10, 11, 15, 23, 34). Studies on the relationship between the number of hippotherapy treatments and the effects on postural balance have not been performed. The present study investigated whether hippotherapy affected seated postural balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance in children with CP. In addition, the effects of 12 versus 24 sessions of hippotherapy on seated postural balance were compared. The hypothesis was that hippotherapy would positively change seated postural balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance, and that 24 sessions of hippotherapy would result in better improvement in seated postural balance compared to 12 sessions. Clinical evidence that hippotherapy improves postural control is strongest in children with cerebral palsy, with measurable gains in static balance, dynamic balance, and alignment/body posture. A systematic review of hippotherapy for postural control in children with cerebral palsy found 8 clinical trials among 264 participants, with most studies having moderate to high methodological quality; the review concluded that hippotherapy can improve postural control, especially static balance in the sitting posture, dynamic balance, and body alignment in children aged 3 to 16 years, particularly those with spastic hemiplegia or diplegia [N2-F1]. A meta-analysis of hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding in children with cerebral palsy similarly states that it is the first known meta-analysis of this literature and that hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding had a statistically significant effect on postural control or balance in this population [N2-F2]. A separate clinical study of 15 children with cerebral palsy reported significant improvements in seated postural balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance after 12 and 24 weeks of hippotherapy, with particularly strong effects after 24 sessions; center of pressure variables such as medio-lateral displacement, anteroposterior displacement, and velocity of displacement all improved, and the Berg Balance Scale and Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory scores also increased [N4-F3]. 

The evidence base is most directly tied to postural control outcomes measured through objective metrics and functional assessments. The clinical study used center of pressure (COP) variables, Berg Balance Scale, and Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory to assess improvements in seated postural balance, dynamic balance, and functional skills [N4-F3]. The systematic review also notes that postural control is measured across several domains, including static balance (especially in the sitting posture), dynamic balance, and alignment/body posture [N2-F1]. The meta-analysis further emphasizes that postural control is organized at two functional levels: direction-specific adjustment and multisensory modulation based on visual, vestibular, and somatosensory input [N2-F2]. This means that the evidence is not limited to a single outcome measure but spans balance, posture, and functional performance.

Strengths of the supporting evidence include the systematic-review quality, the inclusion of clinical trials with moderate-to-high methodological quality, and the direct use of objective measures such as COP and standardized balance scales [N2-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that hippotherapy is most clearly effective in children with cerebral palsy, particularly those with spastic hemiplegia or diplegia [N2-F1][N2-F2]. A limitation is that the evidence base is population-specific: the strongest studies are in children with cerebral palsy, and the review notes that the evidence is focused on this group rather than broad postural-control populations [N2-F1]. The review also notes that the literature on the number of hippotherapy sessions required to change postural balance remains inconclusive, as findings vary from 1 to 40 sessions [N4-F3]. This means the evidence supports hippotherapy as a postural-control intervention, but it does not yet resolve optimal dosage or generalizability beyond children with cerebral palsy.

Repetitive pelvic movements during hippotherapy contribute to postural control by generating rhythmic postural cues and reinforcing stability through movement repetition. The hippotherapy rationale is that the horse’s gait provides a precise, smooth, rhythmic, and repetitive movement pattern similar to human gait, and that the horse’s center of gravity is displaced three-dimensionally during walking, resulting in movement very similar to human pelvic movement during walking [N2-F2]. This rhythmic and repetitive movement pattern is important because it creates a predictable, task-specific sensory environment that can be used to stabilize the rider’s posture. In hippotherapy, the rider must repeatedly adjust to the horse’s movement, which involves using muscles and joint movements over time to increase strength, range of motion, and postural equilibrium responses [N2-F2].

Movement repetition reinforces postural stability by creating a repetitive stimulus that can be learned and adapted. The systematic review states that hippotherapy uses the horse’s movement to promote physical and psychosocial rehabilitation, and that the horse’s movement may facilitate improved contraction, joint stability, weight shift, and postural equilibrium responses in children with cerebral palsy [N2-F2]. The clinical study also emphasizes that repeated hippotherapy sessions can lead to measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance, with especially strong effects after 24 sessions [N4-F3]. This suggests that repetition matters because the same movement pattern is encountered repeatedly, allowing the rider’s postural system to practice and refine postural responses over time.

Biomechanically, rider posture is shaped by the constraints and adaptations associated with the horse’s movement. The horse’s gait displaces the rider’s center of gravity in three dimensions, which forces the rider to engage muscles and joints to maintain balance, as well as to make continuous weight shifts and postural adjustments [N2-F2]. The clinical study notes that the sitting position is used more often by children with cerebral palsy during daily activities, and that this position is similar to the one used during hippotherapy [N4-F3]. This is relevant because the rider’s posture during riding is constrained by the seated position and the horse’s movement pattern, which in turn drives adaptations such as increased strength, joint stability, and postural equilibrium [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that repetitive pelvic movements during hippotherapy do not just mimic human gait; they create a biomechanically relevant training environment that shapes rider posture through repeated adaptation to rhythmic movement.

## Integrated explanation of how hippotherapy enhances postural control

Hippotherapy enhances postural control through a combination of repetitive movement, sensory input, therapist-guided adaptation, and neurophysiological learning. The core idea is that the horse’s rhythmic gait creates a predictable, task-specific movement environment that the rider learns to adapt to, which in turn strengthens postural stability, balance, and coordination.

### 1) Repetitive pelvic movements provide rhythmic postural cues and reinforce stability

The repetitive and rhythmic nature of the horse’s gait is central to hippotherapy. The systematic review states that the horse’s movement is described as precise, smooth, rhythmic, and repetitive, and that the horse’s center of gravity is displaced three-dimensionally during walking, resulting in movement very similar to human pelvic movement during walking [N2-F2]. This is important because it creates a consistent rhythm that can act as a postural cue. Riders repeatedly experience the same movement pattern, which helps them anticipate and adjust to the horse’s motion rather than constantly reacting to unpredictable change [N2-F2].

Repeated exposure to this rhythmic movement reinforces postural stability over time. The systematic review notes that hippotherapy uses the horse’s movement to promote physical rehabilitation and that the horse’s movement may facilitate improved contraction, joint stability, weight shift, and postural equilibrium responses [N2-F2]. The clinical study also reports that repeated hippotherapy sessions can lead to measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance, with especially strong effects after 24 sessions [N4-F3]. This suggests that repetition matters: the rider’s postural system is repeatedly engaged, allowing it to practice and refine responses.

### 2) Balance adjustments and proprioceptive feedback drive postural learning

During hippotherapy, the rider is constantly adjusting to the horse’s movement, which involves continuous sensory feedback and proprioceptive input. The systematic review explains that postural control is organized at two functional levels: direction-specific adjustment when the body is endangered, and multisensory modulation based on visual, vestibular, and somatosensory input [N2-F2]. It also notes that the second level of postural control involves fine-tuning basic adjustments through multisensory afferent input, including changing the order of muscle recruitment, modifying muscle contraction size, and altering antagonist activation [N2-F2]. This means that the rider is not just passively sitting; they are actively sensing and responding to movement.

The clinical study supports this by showing that the rider must use muscles and joint movements over time to increase strength, range of motion, and postural equilibrium responses [N2-F2]. In other words, the rider’s body adapts to the horse’s motion, which strengthens postural control. The repeated sessions also improve seated postural balance and functional performance, indicating that the rider’s ability to adjust to movement improves with practice [N4-F3].

### 3) Neurophysiological mechanisms support motor learning and generalization

Neurophysiologically, movement repetition supports motor learning and neural adaptation by repeatedly engaging the sensory-motor system. The review material describes postural control as a central nervous system process that regulates sensory information from visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems to produce motor output [N3-R2]. It also states that the foundation for skilled performance lies in the ability to match and integrate neural systems, particularly visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems [N3-R3]. This means that hippotherapy is not just a mechanical intervention; it is a form of repetitive training that strengthens neural integration and adaptation.

Sensory feedback, proprioception, and cortical plasticity are all central to this process. The systematic review emphasizes that multisensory input is used to modulate postural adjustment [N2-F2], while the clinical study notes that the rider’s responses include improved contraction, joint stability, weight shift, and postural equilibrium [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the idea that repeated movement exposure strengthens cortical plasticity and the ability to integrate sensory information into motor output [N3-R2][N3-R3].

Balance adjustments during riding may generalize to daily postural control because the rider’s nervous system learns the same principles of multisensory integration and movement coordination in different contexts. The systematic review notes that postural control is organized around direction-specific adjustment and multisensory modulation, and that the CNS uses experiences and environment to control these systems [N2-F2]. The clinical study also states that the sitting position is used more often by children with cerebral palsy during daily activities and that this position is similar to the one used during hippotherapy [N4-F3]. This suggests that the skills learned during riding can transfer to everyday sitting balance and functional performance.

### 4) Therapist manipulation and rider positioning shape movement coordination

Rider adaptation and coordination during hippotherapy are shaped by therapist manipulation and rider positioning. The systematic review explicitly states that the therapist will manipulate the horse’s movements as well as the rider’s position to attain functional outcomes in balance and other areas [N2-F2]. This means the therapist is not simply watching; they are actively shaping the movement environment to target postural goals.

Therapist manipulation also influences movement coordination because the instructor decides whether the horse remains stationary or walks, whether a saddle is used, and how the rider interacts with the horse [N2-F2]. This is important because it allows the therapist to adjust the difficulty and focus of the session, thereby influencing how the rider adapts. The clinical study further supports this by showing that repeated sessions can lead to measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance, indicating that coordinated, therapist-guided practice drives adaptation [N4-F3].

### 5) Movement tempo and rhythmicity affect postural engagement

The rhythmicity and tempo of the horse’s gait are important for postural engagement. The systematic review emphasizes that the horse’s gait is precise, smooth, rhythmic, and repetitive [N2-F2]. This rhythm provides a predictable pattern that the rider can anticipate and respond to, which reduces the cognitive load of constantly reacting to movement and allows more attention to be devoted to postural control [N2-F2]. The clinical study’s focus on seated postural balance and repeated sessions also supports the idea that rhythmic movement can be used repeatedly to strengthen postural engagement [N4-F3].

### 6) Clinical evidence supports postural control gains in specific populations

The strongest clinical evidence for hippotherapy improving postural control comes from children with cerebral palsy. A systematic review of hippotherapy for postural control in children with cerebral palsy found 8 clinical trials among 264 participants, with most studies having moderate to high methodological quality; the review concluded that hippotherapy can improve postural control, especially static balance in the sitting posture, dynamic balance, and body alignment in children aged 3 to 16 years, particularly those with spastic hemiplegia or diplegia [N2-F1]. A meta-analysis of hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding in children with cerebral palsy similarly found a statistically significant effect on postural control or balance in this population [N2-F2].

A separate clinical study of 15 children with cerebral palsy reported significant improvements in seated postural balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance after 12 and 24 weeks of hippotherapy, with particularly strong effects after 24 sessions [N4-F3]. Objective measures such as center of pressure variables—medio-lateral displacement, anteroposterior displacement, and velocity of displacement—also improved [N4-F3]. This shows that hippotherapy is not only associated with subjective improvement; it can be measured using objective balance metrics and functional performance scales.

### 7) Strengths and limitations of the evidence

The evidence base is strongest when it is systematic and includes clinical trials with moderate-to-high methodological quality [N2-F1]. The systematic review and meta-analysis provide broad support for the effectiveness of hippotherapy in children with cerebral palsy [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The clinical study provides direct evidence of measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance [N4-F3]. However, the evidence is population-specific: the strongest studies are in children with cerebral palsy, and the review notes that the literature on the number of hippotherapy sessions required to change postural balance remains inconclusive [N2-F1][N4-F3]. This means the evidence supports hippotherapy as a postural-control intervention, but it does not yet resolve optimal dosage or generalizability beyond children with cerebral palsy.

### 8) Biomechanical constraints and adaptations relevant to rider posture

The biomechanical context of hippotherapy is important because the horse’s movement imposes constraints and drives adaptations. The horse’s gait displaces the rider’s center of gravity in three dimensions, forcing the rider to engage muscles and joints to maintain balance and make continuous weight shifts and postural adjustments [N2-F2]. The clinical study notes that the sitting position is used more often by children with cerebral palsy during daily activities, and that this position is similar to the one used during hippotherapy [N4-F3]. This is relevant because the rider’s posture is constrained by the seated position and the horse’s movement pattern, which in turn drives adaptations such as increased strength, joint stability, and postural equilibrium [N2-F2].

### Bottom line

Taken together, hippotherapy enhances postural control by combining repetitive rhythmic movement, therapist-guided adaptation, and multisensory feedback. The horse’s gait provides a predictable, task-specific rhythm that the rider learns to anticipate and adjust to, which reinforces postural stability over time [N2-F2][N4-F3]. This movement environment engages sensory integration, proprioception, and cortical plasticity, supporting motor learning and neural adaptation [N3-R2][N3-R3]. Therapist manipulation and rider positioning shape how the movement is experienced, while the tempo and rhythmicity of the horse’s gait affect how deeply the rider engages with postural control [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The strongest clinical evidence comes from children with cerebral palsy, showing measurable improvements in static balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how hippotherapy enhances postural control

Hippotherapy enhances postural control through a combination of repetitive movement, sensory input, therapist-guided adaptation, and neurophysiological learning. The core idea is that the horse’s rhythmic gait creates a predictable, task-specific movement environment that the rider learns to adapt to, which in turn strengthens postural stability, balance, and coordination.

### 1) Repetitive pelvic movements provide rhythmic postural cues and reinforce stability

The repetitive and rhythmic nature of the horse’s gait is central to hippotherapy. The systematic review states that the horse’s movement is described as precise, smooth, rhythmic, and repetitive, and that the horse’s center of gravity is displaced three-dimensionally during walking, resulting in movement very similar to human pelvic movement during walking [N2-F2]. This is important because it creates a consistent rhythm that can act as a postural cue. Riders repeatedly experience the same movement pattern, which helps them anticipate and adjust to the horse’s motion rather than constantly reacting to unpredictable change [N2-F2].

Repeated exposure to this rhythmic movement reinforces postural stability over time. The systematic review notes that hippotherapy uses the horse’s movement to promote physical rehabilitation and that the horse’s movement may facilitate improved contraction, joint stability, weight shift, and postural equilibrium responses [N2-F2]. The clinical study also reports that repeated hippotherapy sessions can lead to measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance, with especially strong effects after 24 sessions [N4-F3]. This suggests that repetition matters: the rider’s postural system is repeatedly engaged, allowing it to practice and refine responses.

### 2) Balance adjustments and proprioceptive feedback drive postural learning

During hippotherapy, the rider is constantly adjusting to the horse’s movement, which involves continuous sensory feedback and proprioceptive input. The systematic review explains that postural control is organized at two functional levels: direction-specific adjustment when the body is endangered, and multisensory modulation based on visual, vestibular, and somatosensory input [N2-F2]. It also notes that the second level of postural control involves fine-tuning basic adjustments through multisensory afferent input, including changing the order of muscle recruitment, modifying muscle contraction size, and altering antagonist activation [N2-F2]. This means that the rider is not just passively sitting; they are actively sensing and responding to movement.

The clinical study supports this by showing that the rider must use muscles and joint movements over time to increase strength, range of motion, and postural equilibrium responses [N2-F2]. In other words, the rider’s body adapts to the horse’s motion, which strengthens postural control. The repeated sessions also improve seated postural balance and functional performance, indicating that the rider’s ability to adjust to movement improves with practice [N4-F3].

### 3) Neurophysiological mechanisms support motor learning and generalization

Neurophysiologically, movement repetition supports motor learning and neural adaptation by repeatedly engaging the sensory-motor system. The review material describes postural control as a central nervous system process that regulates sensory information from visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems to produce motor output [N3-R2]. It also states that the foundation for skilled performance lies in the ability to match and integrate neural systems, particularly visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems [N3-R3]. This means that hippotherapy is not just a mechanical intervention; it is a form of repetitive training that strengthens neural integration and adaptation.

Sensory feedback, proprioception, and cortical plasticity are all central to this process. The systematic review emphasizes that multisensory input is used to modulate postural adjustment [N2-F2], while the clinical study notes that the rider’s responses include improved contraction, joint stability, weight shift, and postural equilibrium [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the idea that repeated movement exposure strengthens cortical plasticity and the ability to integrate sensory information into motor output [N3-R2][N3-R3].

Balance adjustments during riding may generalize to daily postural control because the rider’s nervous system learns the same principles of multisensory integration and movement coordination in different contexts. The systematic review notes that postural control is organized around direction-specific adjustment and multisensory modulation, and that the CNS uses experiences and environment to control these systems [N2-F2]. The clinical study also states that the sitting position is used more often by children with cerebral palsy during daily activities and that this position is similar to the one used during hippotherapy [N4-F3]. This suggests that the skills learned during riding can transfer to everyday sitting balance and functional performance.

### 4) Therapist manipulation and rider positioning shape movement coordination

Rider adaptation and coordination during hippotherapy are shaped by therapist manipulation and rider positioning. The systematic review explicitly states that the therapist will manipulate the horse’s movements as well as the rider’s position to attain functional outcomes in balance and other areas [N2-F2]. This means the therapist is not simply watching; they are actively shaping the movement environment to target postural goals.

Therapist manipulation also influences movement coordination because the instructor decides whether the horse remains stationary or walks, whether a saddle is used, and how the rider interacts with the horse [N2-F2]. This is important because it allows the therapist to adjust the difficulty and focus of the session, thereby influencing how the rider adapts. The clinical study further supports this by showing that repeated sessions can lead to measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance, indicating that coordinated, therapist-guided practice drives adaptation [N4-F3].

### 5) Movement tempo and rhythmicity affect postural engagement

The rhythmicity and tempo of the horse’s gait are important for postural engagement. The systematic review emphasizes that the horse’s gait is precise, smooth, rhythmic, and repetitive [N2-F2]. This rhythm provides a predictable pattern that the rider can anticipate and respond to, which reduces the cognitive load of constantly reacting to movement and allows more attention to be devoted to postural control [N2-F2]. The clinical study’s focus on seated postural balance and repeated sessions also supports the idea that rhythmic movement can be used repeatedly to strengthen postural engagement [N4-F3].

### 6) Clinical evidence supports postural control gains in specific populations

The strongest clinical evidence for hippotherapy improving postural control comes from children with cerebral palsy. A systematic review of hippotherapy for postural control in children with cerebral palsy found 8 clinical trials among 264 participants, with most studies having moderate to high methodological quality; the review concluded that hippotherapy can improve postural control, especially static balance in the sitting posture, dynamic balance, and body alignment in children aged 3 to 16 years, particularly those with spastic hemiplegia or diplegia [N2-F1]. A meta-analysis of hippotherapy and therapeutic horseback riding in children with cerebral palsy similarly found a statistically significant effect on postural control or balance in this population [N2-F2].

Objective measures such as center of pressure variables—medio-lateral displacement, anteroposterior displacement, and velocity of displacement—also improved [N4-F3]. This shows that hippotherapy is not only associated with subjective improvement; it can be measured using objective balance metrics and functional performance scales.

### 7) Strengths and limitations of the evidence

The evidence base is strongest when it is systematic and includes clinical trials with moderate-to-high methodological quality [N2-F1]. The systematic review and meta-analysis provide broad support for the effectiveness of hippotherapy in children with cerebral palsy [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The clinical study provides direct evidence of measurable improvements in seated postural balance and functional performance [N4-F3]. However, the evidence is population-specific: the strongest studies are in children with cerebral palsy, and the review notes that the literature on the number of hippotherapy sessions required to change postural balance remains inconclusive [N2-F1][N4-F3]. This means the evidence supports hippotherapy as a postural-control intervention, but it does not yet resolve optimal dosage or generalizability beyond children with cerebral palsy.

### 8) Biomechanical constraints and adaptations relevant to rider posture

The biomechanical context of hippotherapy is important because the horse’s movement imposes constraints and drives adaptations. The horse’s gait displaces the rider’s center of gravity in three dimensions, forcing the rider to engage muscles and joints to maintain balance and make continuous weight shifts and postural adjustments [N2-F2]. The clinical study notes that the sitting position is used more often by children with cerebral palsy during daily activities, and that this position is similar to the one used during hippotherapy [N4-F3]. This is relevant because the rider’s posture is constrained by the seated position and the horse’s movement pattern, which in turn drives adaptations such as increased strength, joint stability, and postural equilibrium [N2-F2].

### Bottom line

Taken together, hippotherapy enhances postural control by combining repetitive rhythmic movement, therapist-guided adaptation, and multisensory feedback. The horse’s gait provides a predictable, task-specific rhythm that the rider learns to anticipate and adjust to, which reinforces postural stability over time [N2-F2][N4-F3]. This movement environment engages sensory integration, proprioception, and cortical plasticity, supporting motor learning and neural adaptation [N3-R2][N3-R3]. Therapist manipulation and rider positioning shape how the movement is experienced, while the tempo and rhythmicity of the horse’s gait affect how deeply the rider engages with postural control [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The strongest clinical evidence comes from children with cerebral palsy, showing measurable improvements in static balance, dynamic balance, and functional performance [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].
